questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes an open ecosystem from a closed system?

options.text: An open ecosystem exchanges energy and matter, while a closed system exchanges energy but not matter
options.why: The distinction concerns what crosses the boundary. Most ecosystems receive and release both energy and matter.

options.text: An open ecosystem exchanges matter but retains energy, while a closed system releases energy as heat
options.why: Open ecosystems exchange energy as well as matter. Light can enter and heat can leave.

options.text: An open ecosystem exchanges energy only, while a closed system exchanges matter only
options.why: Those categories are reversed and split in a way the definitions don’t support. Closed systems can exchange energy but not matter.

options.text: An open ecosystem has unlimited inputs, while a closed system has no inputs of any kind
options.why: Open doesn’t mean unlimited. A closed system can still receive or release energy.

questions.stem: Which process can provide the external energy source for an ecosystem below the level of light penetration?

options.text: Oxidation of inorganic substances by chemoautotrophs
options.why: Chemoautotrophs capture energy released by oxidation reactions. That allows carbon fixation without sunlight.

options.text: Absorption of heat by heterotrophs from deep water
options.why: Heterotrophs obtain carbon compounds from other organisms. Environmental heat isn’t their energy source for building biomass.

options.text: Digestion of dead organisms by photoautotrophs
options.why: Photoautotrophs use light and inorganic carbon. Digestion of dead material describes heterotrophic feeding.

options.text: Conversion of carbon dioxide into light by decomposers
options.why: Decomposers obtain carbon and energy from organic matter. They don’t convert carbon dioxide into light.

questions.stem: In the food chain grass → vole → owl, what does the arrow from the vole to the owl represent?

options.text: Transfer of energy and biomass from the vole to the owl
options.why: Food-chain arrows point from food to consumer. Energy and organic matter pass to the owl when it eats the vole.

options.text: Movement of the owl toward the vole during hunting
options.why: Arrows don’t show physical movement. They show the direction of energy and biomass transfer.

options.text: Transfer of respiratory heat from the owl to the vole
options.why: Respiratory heat passes to the environment. It isn’t transferred backwards to the prey.

options.text: Cycling of energy from the owl back into the vole population
options.why: Energy doesn’t cycle back to earlier trophic levels. It flows through the chain and becomes dispersed as heat.

questions.stem: Which feeding process identifies an organism as a decomposer rather than a detritivore?

options.text: Secreting enzymes onto dead organic matter and absorbing soluble products
options.why: Decomposers digest organic matter externally and then absorb the products. Many fungi and bacteria feed this way.

options.text: Ingesting fragments of dead organic matter and digesting them internally
options.why: That describes a detritivore. Its digestion occurs after the dead material has been ingested.

options.text: Capturing living prey and digesting the tissues inside a gut
options.why: That describes predatory heterotrophic feeding. The food is living prey rather than dead organic matter.

options.text: Using light energy to synthesize carbon compounds from carbon dioxide
options.why: That describes photoautotrophy. Decomposers obtain organic carbon from dead material.

questions.stem: Why do autotrophs carry out cell respiration?

options.text: To transfer energy from carbon compounds to ATP for cellular work
options.why: Autotrophs need ATP for their cellular processes. They can respire carbon compounds that they synthesized themselves.

options.text: To obtain all of their carbon compounds by consuming heterotrophs
options.why: Obtaining organic compounds from other organisms defines heterotrophy. Autotrophs build carbon compounds from inorganic substances.

options.text: To convert heat from the environment directly into chemical energy
options.why: Cells don’t use environmental heat as a direct energy source for ATP production. Respiration oxidizes carbon compounds.

options.text: To replace photosynthesis whenever sufficient light energy is available
options.why: Respiration and photosynthesis have different roles and can occur during the same period. Respiration doesn’t replace photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Primary consumers receive 360 kJ m−2 yr−1 from producers containing 4,500 kJ m−2 yr−1. What is the transfer efficiency?

options.why: The calculation is 360 divided by 4,500, multiplied by 100. That gives 8%.
This comes from dividing the larger value by the smaller one without using the transfer-efficiency formula. The received energy must be the numerator.
A decimal-place error produces this value. The fraction transferred is 0.08, which becomes 8%.
Subtracting the values finds an energy difference, not a percentage efficiency. A ratio between adjacent levels is required.

questions.stem: Which event makes chemical energy unavailable to the next consumer trophic level while transferring it to the environment as heat?

options.text: Oxidation of carbon compounds during cell respiration
options.why: Respiration transfers some chemical energy to ATP, and energy becomes dispersed as heat when ATP is produced and used.

options.text: Storage of carbon compounds in newly formed consumer biomass
options.why: Energy retained in new biomass can remain available to a consumer at the next trophic level.

options.text: Movement of a consumer from one habitat into another
options.why: Movement can transport biomass between places, but it doesn’t by itself explain conversion of chemical energy to heat.

options.text: Assimilation of digested molecules into new body tissues
options.why: Assimilation stores matter and chemical energy in biomass. That biomass may later be eaten.

questions.stem: Which label and unit are appropriate for a pyramid of energy?

options.text: Energy transferred per trophic level, measured in kJ m−2 yr−1
options.why: An energy pyramid represents energy per unit area per unit time. Its bars therefore always narrow toward the top.

options.text: Standing biomass at each trophic level, measured in grams at one time
options.why: That would describe a biomass measurement. It lacks the energy unit and time component needed for an energy pyramid.

options.text: Population size at each trophic level, measured as organisms per year
options.why: Population size belongs in a pyramid of numbers. Counting organisms doesn’t measure their energy transfer.

options.text: Energy density of individual organisms, measured in kJ g−1 yr−1
options.why: An energy pyramid shows total transfer across an area, not the energy content of each gram of an organism.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes secondary production?

options.text: It is the accumulation of carbon compounds in heterotroph biomass
options.why: Secondary production includes biomass accumulated by heterotrophs at any consumer level.

options.text: It is the biomass accumulated only by organisms classified as secondary consumers
options.why: The word “secondary” doesn’t name a trophic level here. Primary, secondary and tertiary consumers can all contribute.

options.text: It is the total carbon dioxide released by heterotrophs during cell respiration
options.why: Respired carbon has left biomass. Production counts carbon compounds accumulated in new biomass.

options.text: It is the carbon fixed from inorganic substances by photoautotrophs and chemoautotrophs
options.why: Accumulation by autotrophs is primary production. Secondary production belongs to heterotrophs.

questions.stem: During one year, photosynthesis in a forest removes more carbon dioxide than respiration and combustion release. How should the forest be classified for that year?

options.text: A carbon sink, because it has net carbon uptake
options.why: Uptake exceeds release during the measured period, so carbon accumulates in the system.

options.text: A carbon source, because every organism in the forest respires
options.why: Respiration releases carbon dioxide, but classification depends on the net balance. Here photosynthetic uptake is greater.

options.text: A closed system, because its carbon remains inside its boundary
options.why: Carbon dioxide crosses the forest boundary, so the forest remains open. Net uptake doesn’t make a system closed.

options.text: A chemoautotrophic system, because carbon compounds accumulate in biomass
options.why: Chemoautotrophy describes an organism’s energy source. It doesn’t describe the net carbon balance of a forest.

questions.stem: What best explains the annual oscillation in the Keeling Curve?

options.text: Seasonal changes in the balance between photosynthesis and respiration, especially in the Northern Hemisphere
options.why: Carbon dioxide generally falls during the Northern Hemisphere growing season and rises when photosynthesis declines relative to respiration and decomposition.

options.text: A yearly reversal in which combustion removes carbon dioxide during summer and releases it during winter
options.why: Combustion releases carbon dioxide in every season. It doesn’t reverse direction during summer.

options.text: Seasonal conversion of atmospheric carbon dioxide into oxygen by animal cell respiration
options.why: Animal respiration consumes oxygen and releases carbon dioxide. Photosynthesis is the process that removes carbon dioxide.

options.text: A yearly change in the amount of carbon stored permanently in coal and oil deposits
options.why: Fossil-fuel stores don’t expand and contract enough each year to cause the oscillation. Seasonal biological activity does.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares the movement of energy and chemical elements through an ecosystem?

options.text: Energy flows through and becomes dispersed as heat, while chemical elements are recycled
options.why: Energy requires a continuing external supply, usually sunlight. Atoms can return to the environment and be used again.

options.text: Energy and chemical elements both cycle back to producers after each feeding transfer
options.why: Elements can cycle back to producers, but energy can’t. Much of it becomes dispersed as heat.

options.text: Energy is recycled by decomposers, while chemical elements leave permanently in respiratory heat
options.why: Heat is an energy transfer, not a chemical element. Decomposers recycle elements but don’t recycle energy.

options.text: Energy remains stored in ecosystems, while only carbon must be continually replaced
options.why: Ecosystems need continuing energy input. Carbon and other required chemical elements are recycled.
